disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating accompanied by a sense of loss of control, followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives or diuretics, fasting, or excessive exercise. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body weight and shape, but individuals are typically of normal weight or overweight, distinguishing it from classic presentations of anorexia nervosa. The course is often fluctuating, with periods of more frequent episodes during times of stress, transitions, or weight-focused environments, and it commonly co-occurs with mood and anxiety symptoms. Clinically, it is differentiated from binge-eating disorder by the presence of compensatory behaviors and from non-pathological overeating by the recurrent, intrusive nature of the behaviors and associated distress and impairment.

narrative.stressor: About eight months ago, Manuel started staying late at the shop to prepare for his ASE Master Diesel exams and to help pilot a new electric truck service line, which meant long days on his feet, skipped meals, and grabbing fast food between jobs. A younger technician he was mentoring began posting gym selfies and "lean bulking" tips in their group chat, and the shop culture subtly shifted toward comparing how "in shape" everyone looked, which made Manuel self-conscious about the weight he’d slowly put on since high school while still eating heavy Midwestern comfort foods and Oktoberfest fare. To cope with the mounting pressure from certification prep, overtime, and his own perfectionism, he fell into a pattern of coming home exhausted, zoning out with simulation games and late-night Bengals highlights, and eating large amounts of whatever was easy to make or order, followed by increasingly rigid efforts the next day to "undo" it. Over about six months this cycle intensified, began to interfere with his soccer performance and weekend hikes, and he finally agreed to see a mental health provider after his primary care doctor, concerned about erratic weight changes and his description of "making up" for nights of overeating, suggested a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m constantly trying to make up for eating too much, and it’s taking over how I plan my days.”

narrative.stressor: Daphne’s difficulties around food became more intense after she returned from a trip to Kyoto about a year ago, where she was struck by how slim and put-together many people looked compared to how she saw herself in photos from the trip. Back home in Okanogan County, she threw herself into eco-fashion projects and online art communities, many of which emphasized minimalism and "clean eating" aesthetics that made her increasingly critical of her own body when she compared it to stylized images of other textile artists. During a particularly stressful period at the shop—juggling a rush of wedding garments, vendor disputes, and late-night dye experiments—she began coping by eating large, improvised meals alone in her small kitchen after work, then feeling panicked about the impact on her body and taking drastic measures to counteract it. Over six months, this cycle escalated, she withdrew from hikes and yoga classes out of embarrassment about how she looked, and a close friend from her local art center finally urged her to seek psychiatric help after Daphne confided that her eating and efforts to control her weight felt "out of control" and were crowding out her art and sleep.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Once I start eating in the evenings, it feels like I can’t stop or control it at all.”

narrative.stressor: For Ace, problems around eating began to stand out after the birth of his second child, when family dinners became rushed and chaotic and he picked up more closing shifts at the store to cover extra expenses. His parents and in-laws, worried about his long hours and making frequent comments about "watching his health" in middle age, started remarking on small weight changes at family gatherings, which clashed with his own desire to appear balanced and in control as the family’s steady provider. In response, he fell into a pattern of quietly overeating during late-night meals after work and then relying on strict rules and compensatory routines the following days to try to get back to what he thought he "should" weigh, all while presenting an easygoing, harmonious front to his wife and kids. When his wife noticed he was increasingly preoccupied with how his clothes fit, avoiding certain family meals, and seemed unusually distressed after looking at photos from a lake hike, she gently encouraged him to talk to their primary care physician, who then referred him to psychiatry after Ace described how much his self-worth now hinged on his body size.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I feel like how I see myself depends almost completely on what I weigh or how my body looks.”
